nodes.characterization_summary: SEM reveals needle-like structure of Ru/CoP with numerous small nanoparticles growing on the needle-like branches.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) observations reveal that the prepared Ru/CoP maintains its original needle-like structure, with numerous small nanoparticles growing on the needle-like branches (Fig. 2a and b).

nodes.characterization_summary: TEM confirms needle-like structure of Ru/CoP with small particles; inset shows partial enlarged drawing.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) observations reveal that the prepared Ru/CoP maintains its original needle-like structure, with numerous small nanoparticles growing on the needle-like branches (Fig. 2a and b).

nodes.characterization_summary: HRTEM shows clear phases and interfaces between Ru and CoP; lattice distance of 0.19 nm corresponds to (211) planes of CoP; FFT confirms hcp structure of Ru with ABAB atomic arrangement.
nodes.evidence_snippet: We then investigated the existence of a heterointerface between Ru and CoP using high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM), where clear phases and interfaces between them are observed (Fig. 2c). In these phases, the lattice distance of 0.19 nm in area 1 corresponds to the (211) planes of CoP, while the fast Fourier transformation (FFT) image in area 2 shows the hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structure of Ru with an ABAB atomic arrangement.

nodes.characterization_summary: XPS shows Co–P peak negative shift in Ru/CoP and Ru/CoP-B compared to CoP, indicating electronic interactions between Ru and CoP; Co LMM spectrum confirms coexistence of Co²⁺ and Co³⁺ in Ru/CoP.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As shown in Fig. S18 (ESI†), the Co–P peak in Ru/CoP and Ru/CoP–B exhibits a negative shift compared to CoP, indicating electronic interactions between Ru and CoP.43 Meanwhile, the result of Co LMM spectrum confirms the coexistence of Co²⁺ and Co³⁺ in Ru/CoP (Fig. S19a, ESI†).

nodes.characterization_summary: SERS confirms presence of Ru-P bonds in Ru/CoP, proving Ru nanoparticles interact with CoP through P atoms.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In addition, surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) was employed to investigate the bonding state between Ru and CoP. The presence of Ru-P bonds in Ru/CoP proves that Ru nanoparticles interact with CoP through the P atoms in CoP (Fig. S19b, ESI†).

nodes.characterization_summary: UPS confirms CoP has larger work function than Ru, consistent with theoretical calculations indicating electron transfer from Ru to CoP.
nodes.evidence_snippet: To verify the electronic interaction, we conducted ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS) tests. As shown in Fig. S20 (ESI†), CoP has a larger work function than Ru, which is consistent with the results of our theoretical calculations, indicating that electrons are transferred from Ru to CoP.

nodes.characterization_summary: ICP analysis determines Ru content as 0.12 wt% in Ru/CoP and 0.23 wt% in Ru/CoP-B.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Meanwhile, the content of Ru in Ru/CoP and Ru/CoP–B was determined via inductively coupled plasma (ICP) analysis (the content of Ru in Ru/CoP and Ru/CoP–B was 0.12 wt% and 0.23 wt%, respectively)

nodes.characterization_summary: In situ Raman spectroscopy reveals interfacial water structure in Ru/CoP with bands at 3200-3600 cm⁻¹ corresponding to H₂O stretching modes; peaks at ~3200, ~3400, and ~3600 cm⁻¹ represent 4·HB·H₂O, 2-HB·H₂O, and K⁺·H₂O respectively.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As shown in Fig. 4a, the bands at 3200-3600 cm⁻¹ correspond to the stretching modes of H₂O, where the peaks around 3200, 3400, and 3600 cm⁻¹ represent 4·HB·H₂O, 2-HB·H₂O, and K⁺·H₂O, respectively.26,27

nodes.characterization_summary: KPFM shows Ru/CoP exhibits the largest surface potential (Es), indicating a stronger built-in electric field.
nodes.evidence_snippet: To elucidate the existence of built-in electric field, Kelvin Probe Force Microscopy (KPFM) was performed. As shown in Fig. 4h and Fig. S56 (ESI†), Ru/CoP exhibits the largest surface potential (Es), indicating a stronger built-in electric field.

nodes.characterization_summary: In situ SERS with SCN⁻ as reporter shows larger Stark tuning rate for Ru/CoP compared to Ru/CoP-B, confirming stronger local electric field in needle-like structure.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Herein, we utilized in situ SERS with SCN⁻ as a reporter to detect the local electric field induced by the needle-like Ru/CoP (Fig. S48, ESI†). As depicted in Fig. 4d, Ru/CoP exhibits a larger Stark tuning rate compared to Ru/CoP-B, which implies the presence of a stronger electric field in Ru/CoP.

nodes.characterization_summary: EIS shows Ru/CoP has largest Cφ (∗H adsorption pseudo-capacitance) values at different overpotentials compared to Ru/CoP-B and CoP, indicating greatest ∗H production.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Subsequently, we evaluated the amount of ∗H on these electrocatalysts during the HER using EIS at various overpotentials (Fig. S53, ESI†). ... As illustrated in Fig. 4f, Ru/CoP exhibits the largest Cφ at different overpotentials when compared to Ru/CoP-B and CoP, indicating the greatest production of ∗H.
